column2: Drought impact on ecosystems in Europe
column7: Soil moisture deficit index; annual anomaly from 1995–2019 long-term mean; % of ecosystem area affected
column8: EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; 8th EAP adaptation objective; EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS); ERA5 reanalysis soil moisture data; ECMWF meteorological driver data; remote sensing vegetation productivity (NDVI, FAPAR)

The indicator uses ERA5 reanalysis soil moisture data and CLMS remote sensing — all direct climate data products. The EMEP meteorological driver (ECMWF) is a direct input to the deposition model. Score 3: weather/climate data are the primary and explicit calculation input.

column2: Economic losses from weather and climate-related extreme events in Europe
column7: EUR billion/year (2024 prices); annual total economic losses
column8: EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; 8th EAP adaptation objective; EU Civil Protection Mechanism; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Munich Re NatCatSERVICE database; Swiss Re sigma; national disaster registries; Eurostat GDP deflator for price adjustment
column12: Directly measures monetary damages caused by weather and climate events. The indicator is entirely constituted of climate/weather impact data — flood losses, storm damage, heatwave costs, drought impacts. Each loss event is classified by meteorological hazard type (hydrological 47%, meteorological 27%, climatological 26%). Weather data determine both the occurrence and magnitude of the measured losses.

column2: Extreme heat events — frequency and intensity in Europe
column7: Days per year above 35°C; heatwave frequency index; excess mortality during heatwaves

E-OBS observational gridded temperature data and C3S ERA5 reanalysis are the primary inputs. Heat impacts on ecosystems (tree mortality, coral bleaching, crop failure) are directly mediated by temperature extremes. Score 3: temperature data are the exclusive calculation input.

column9: EA/NRW/SEPA Water Framework Directive reporting

column2: GHG emissions per capita (t CO₂e)
column7: tonnes CO₂ equivalent per capita per year

column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment
column12: GHG emissions are the primary cause of climate change and hence the highest-level climate driver of biodiversity loss; this indicator IS a climate variable.

column2: Global and European temperatures
column7: °C anomaly vs 1850–1900 pre-industrial average; decadal means
column8: EU Climate Law 2021 (1.5°C goal); Paris Agreement; 8th EAP mitigation objective; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) ERA5 reanalysis; HadCRUT5 (UK Met Office / CRU); GISTEMP; Berkeley Earth; NOAA GlobalTemp
column12: This IS a climate data metric — directly calculated from instrumental temperature records and modelled outputs from GCMs. Global mean surface temperature anomaly data are the primary input. The 2024 dataset confirmed 1.54–1.60°C anomaly, the first calendar year exceeding 1.5°C. Temperature datasets (C3S, HadCRUT5, GISTEMP) are the direct source.

column2: Ocean acidification in European seas
column7: pH units (surface seawater); aragonite saturation state (Ω Ar); trend
column8: MSFD; OSPAR; EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Nature Restoration Law 2024 (marine ecosystems); Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: European marine monitoring networks (OSPAR, EMODnet); Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS); SOCAT (Surface Ocean CO₂ Atlas); Argo float network; national oceanographic institutes
column12: Ocean acidification is directly caused by absorption of atmospheric CO₂ — a consequence of fossil fuel burning and land use change. pH and aragonite saturation are calculated from seawater chemistry measurements (dissolved CO₂, alkalinity, temperature). The degree of acidification is mechanistically linked to atmospheric CO₂ concentrations. Score 3: ocean chemistry observations are the direct input; the phenomenon IS a climate change impact.

column7: Joules (× 10²²) upper 700m ocean heat content anomaly; marine heatwave days per year

column9: Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS); NOAA Argo float array; ESA Climate Change Initiative Sea Surface Temperature; Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) marine data
column12: Ocean heat content is a direct measure of accumulated climate energy in the ocean system. Marine heatwaves are defined by sea surface temperature exceedance relative to a seasonal climatology — entirely temperature-driven. CMEMS and Argo observational datasets are direct inputs. Score 3: ocean temperature data are the sole calculation input and the indicator IS a measure of climate impact.

column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment

column8: EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; MSFD Good Environmental Status; EU Maritime Spatial Planning Directive; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity; Restore and enhance nature's contributions to people

column2: Share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption
column7: % of gross final energy consumption from renewable sources
column8: EU Renewable Energy Directive (recast) 2023 (42.5% target by 2030); 8th EAP sustainability objective Article 2.f; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Eurostat Energy Statistics (SHARES tool); Member State energy balances; ENTSO-E electricity data; Eurostat Short-Term Energy Statistics (STES)
column12: Renewable energy share in any given year is directly dependent on weather: wind speed determines wind power output, solar irradiance determines solar PV, rainfall determines hydropower. Inter-annual variability driven by weather affects the headline % figure significantly (e.g., drought years reduce hydro; low-wind years reduce wind share). Score 3: weather conditions directly determine the annual generation mix.

column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra / UKCEH Countryside Survey soils

column2: Soil moisture deficit — impact on ecosystem productivity
column7: Annual soil moisture anomaly (deviation from 1995–2019 mean); % of ecosystem area affected by deficit
column8: EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; Nature Restoration Law 2024; EU Soil Strategy 2030; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS) Soil Water Index; ERA5 reanalysis soil moisture; ECMWF land surface model outputs; Copernicus Global Land Service FAPAR (fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation)
column12: This indicator is directly derived from ERA5 reanalysis soil moisture data — a climate data product. The soil moisture deficit is calculated as the annual average soil water content relative to a 25-year climatological mean, using meteorological forcing data. Negative anomalies indicate drought stress affecting vegetation productivity. Score 3: ERA5 climate reanalysis data are the primary and explicit calculation input.

column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment
column12: Mechanistic soil carbon models (e.g. RothC, CENTURY, ESMs) use temperature and precipitation as primary drivers; climate projections directly determine future SOC trajectories.

column2: Soil organic carbon content (agricultural and semi-natural land) (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Countryside Survey / NSRI / UKCEH
column12: Soil carbon is highly sensitive to temperature and moisture: warming increases decomposition rates, drought affects carbon inputs. Soil organic carbon underpins productivity resilience and is a key climate adaptation metric.

column2: Species abundance index (terrestrial and freshwater) (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: JNCC/Defra UK Biodiversity Indicators
column12: Species abundance trajectories reflect cumulative pressures including climate change (phenological mismatches, range shifts, novel extremes). This is a key biodiversity-climate interaction indicator.

column2: Spring Index (phenology)
column7: Mean day-of-year of 4 spring events (days after 31 December)
column8: UK Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2025; Environment Act 2021 species targets; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: UK Phenology Network (Nature's Calendar / Woodland Trust); Royal Meteorological Society (historic)
column12: This is an explicitly climate-driven indicator. The Spring Index is the mean day-of-year of 4 phenological events directly correlated with spring temperature (Central England Temperature). Temperature is the primary explanatory variable and the indicator is explicitly analysed against CET.

column2: Spring phenological index — plant and animal responses to climate
column7: Day-of-year (DOY) of key phenophase events; days shift per decade
column8: EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Nature Restoration Law 2024; EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; Halt extinction, recover species; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Pan-European Phenology network (PEP725); MODIS land surface temperature and greenness (NDVI); Copernicus CLMS vegetation phenology products; national phenology monitoring networks
column12: This is explicitly a climate response indicator. Spring phenological events (first leaf, first flowering, bird migration arrival) are directly and mechanistically driven by accumulated spring temperature (growing degree days). Temperature is the primary explanatory variable and the indicator is specifically designed to detect and quantify climate change impacts on biological timing. Score 3.

column2: Temperature anomaly (°C vs 1960–1969)
column7: °C anomaly from 1960–1969 baseline; HadCRUT global mean surface temperature
column8: Kunming-Montreal GBF: Directly relevant to GBF Target 8 (minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity). SDG 13 (Climate Action). This IS the key climate biodiversity pressure driver in IPBES GA.
column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment
column12: Temperature anomaly IS a climate variable; this indicator directly measures the global warming signal that drives biodiversity loss through range shifts, phenological mismatch and extreme events.

column2: Temperature-adjusted buildings sector emissions
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: DESNZ UK GHG Inventory + CCC temperature adjustment
column12: CCC explicitly applies a temperature adjustment (Heating Degree Day regression) to buildings emissions to remove weather effects before assessing policy progress; weather data are a direct, formal input.

column2: UK food self-sufficiency ratio (production to consumption, by food type)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra UK Food Security Report (biennial)
column12: Self-sufficiency reflects capacity to withstand climate-driven domestic and import supply disruptions; weather volatility in major exporting regions is a primary driver of import dependency.

column2: Water stress index in European river basins
column7: Water Exploitation Index Plus (WEI+) — ratio of freshwater abstraction to availability; % of territory in high stress
column8: Water Framework Directive; EU Water Blueprint 2012; EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; Nature Restoration Law 2024 (restore 25,000 km of rivers); Reduce pollution to safe levels; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity; Restore and enhance nature's contributions to people
column9: Eurostat freshwater abstraction statistics; EEA Waterbase WFD reporting; AQUASTAT (FAO); JRC Global Runoff Data Centre; LISFLOOD hydrological model (JRC)
column12: Water availability is directly determined by precipitation and evapotranspiration (temperature-driven). The LISFLOOD hydrological model underlying WEI+ calculations uses ERA5 rainfall and temperature as primary inputs to model river flows and groundwater recharge. Drought years dramatically increase WEI+ scores. Score 3: precipitation and temperature are direct inputs to the water availability model.

column2: Wildfire burned area in Europe
column7: thousand hectares/year; number of fires; economic losses from fires
column8: EU Adaptation Strategy 2021; EU Forest Strategy 2030; Nature Restoration Law 2024; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) / Copernicus Emergency Management Service; JRC fire database; national fire agencies; Sentinel satellite burnt area products
column12: Wildfire occurrence and extent are directly driven by temperature, drought, and wind — all climate/weather variables. The Canadian Fire Weather Index (FWI) system — used by EFFIS — explicitly uses daily temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and precipitation as primary inputs. Score 3: weather data are direct, explicit inputs to the fire danger calculation.

column2: Woodland carbon sequestration (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Forestry Commission National Forest Inventory / NAEI
column12: Forest growth and carbon uptake are strongly weather-dependent: drought, windthrow and pest outbreaks (themselves climate-sensitive) directly affect net sequestration rates.

column2: 10.CY.2 Soil organic carbon stocks
column7: GtC or tC/ha of organic carbon in agricultural soils; trend over time
column8: GBF Target 10 (complementary). Soil carbon as biodiversity indicator and climate mitigation outcome.
column9: ISRIC SoilGrids (https://soilgrids.org); FAO GSOC; national soil monitoring networks
column12: Soil carbon decomposition is temperature-dependent; precipitation affects carbon inputs through plant productivity.

column2: 8.b Number of countries with policies to minimize the impact of climate change and ocean acidification on biodiversity and to minimize negative and foster positive impacts of climate action on biodiversity
column7: Binary governance progress score (0–5) based on 9 questions covering: NBSAP climate/OA actions; climate policies addressing biodiversity; monitoring; types of action (mitigation, adaptation, DRR, NbS); minimising negative/positive climate-action impacts
column8: GBF Target 8 – climate change governance for biodiversity (binary). Directly tracks climate-biodiversity governance nexus. Relevant to SDG 13.2.
column9: CBD national reporting portal; UNFCCC NDC registry; national NBSAPs
column12: Questions explicitly address climate-biodiversity integration; scored 2 because context is directly climate-related even though scoring uses no climate data.

column2: 8.CT.1 Number of countries adopting and implementing national DRR strategies in line with Sendai Framework
column7: Count/% of countries with national DRR strategies aligned to Sendai Framework 2015–2030
column8: GBF Target 8 (component). Resilience governance linking climate change, DRR and biodiversity.
column9: UNDRR Sendai Monitor; national DRR strategies; CBD national reporting
column12: DRR strategies directly address climate disaster risks; governance progress indicator based on policy documents.

column2: 8.CY.1 Above-ground biomass stock in forest (tonnes/ha)
column7: Mean above-ground carbon biomass density (tC/ha) in forests; trend over time
column8: GBF Target 8 (complementary). Forest carbon stocks as indicator of climate regulation capacity.
column9: ESA GlobBiomass; GEDI LiDAR; national forest inventory biomass; FAO FRA
column12: Forest biomass affected by climate-driven fire, drought and temperature-driven productivity changes.

column2: A.CY.19 Red List Index – wild relatives of domesticated animals
column7: RLI (0–1) for wild relatives of domesticated animal species used in food and agriculture
column8: GBF Goal A / T4, T10 (complementary). Genetic resource for food security under climate change.
column9: IUCN Red List; FAO list of wild relatives of domesticated animals; IUCN SSC specialist groups
column12: Wild relatives face climate-driven range contractions; conservation underpins adaptive potential for future climates.

column2: A.CY.7 Global salt marsh extent
column7: Total area (ha) of coastal salt marsh globally; trend over time
column8: GBF Goal A (complementary). Salt marshes as blue carbon habitats under climate threat.
column9: Mcowen et al. 2017 dataset; Blue Carbon Initiative; national coastal habitat surveys; Sentinel-2
column12: Salt marsh extent affected by sea-level rise and coastal squeeze; remote sensing captures climate-driven losses.

column2: Agricultural GHG emissions
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: DESNZ UK GHG Inventory
column12: Agricultural GHG emissions include N2O from soils and CH4 from enteric fermentation; soil N2O is strongly temperature and moisture dependent; IPCC methodology uses climate-informed emission factors.

column2: Beef emissions intensity (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: NAEI / AHDB
column12: Emissions intensity reflects feed conversion, breed, and management; climate moderately affects grass growth quality and thus feed supplementation requirements.

column2: Carbon stocks and fluxes in European forests
column7: Pg C (petagram carbon) in forest biomass and soils; MtC/year net flux; sink strength
column8: EU LULUCF Regulation 2018 (−310 MtCO₂e forest sector target); EU Forest Strategy 2030; EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Paris Agreement land sector; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: National Forest Inventories processed through CBM-CFS3 carbon model; FAO carbon assessment; JRC FISE; IPCC Tier 3 methods where available
column12: Forest carbon flux modelling (e.g., Carbon Budget Model CBM-CFS3, EFISCEN) uses temperature and precipitation to determine growth increments, mortality and decomposition rates. Drought events visibly reduce European forest carbon sinks in recent years (observed in LULUCF data). Score 2: climate parameters are embedded in carbon accounting models.

column2: CGMFC-21 – Continuous Global Mangrove Forest Cover for the 21st Century
column7: Area (ha) of mangrove cover; annual change (%)
column8: SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water): Relevant to SDG 15.1 (conservation of coastal ecosystems); SDG 14.2 (protect marine and coastal ecosystems); SDG 13.1 (climate resilience). GBF Targets 2 and 3.
column9: JAXA Global Mangrove Watch (Landsat/ALOS remote sensing); Hamilton & Casey 2016
column12: Climate change drives sea-level rise and storm damage affecting mangrove distribution.

column2: Coastal carbon-rich habitat
column8: Kunming-Montreal GBF: Relevant to GBF Goal A (biodiversity status and trends) and GBF monitoring framework headline indicators. Informs IPBES Global Assessment chapters on status and trends of nature for SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water).
column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment
column12: Coastal carbon-rich habitats (mangrove, saltmarsh, seagrass) are sensitive to sea-level rise and storm surges; monitoring via remote sensing incorporates weather-driven signal variation.

column2: Communities resilient to flooding and coastal erosion
column7: number of properties better protected; flood risk management outcomes
column8: Environmental Improvement Plan (EIP) 2025; Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF); Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: EA Flood and Coastal Risk Management national outcome measures
column12: Flood resilience measures (properties protected); targets are set partly based on climate change projections and flood risk modelling using climate scenarios.

column2: Emissions for five key air pollutants
column8: Environmental Improvement Plan (EIP) 2025; Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF); Reduce pollution to safe levels
column9: National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (NAEI); Defra Air Quality statistics
column12: Emissions modelled via NAEI activity data × emission factors; temperature affects NH3 volatilisation, but formal weather adjustment applies only to NH3. The NAEI uses meteorological data for deposition modelling components.

column2: Eutrophication caused by atmospheric nitrogen deposition in European ecosystems
column7: % of ecosystem area where critical loads for nitrogen deposition are exceeded
column8: EU National Emission Ceilings (NEC) Directive 2016; EU Farm to Fork Strategy (−50% nutrient losses); EU Zero Pollution Action Plan; Nature Restoration Law 2024; Reduce pollution to safe levels
column9: EMEP atmospheric dispersion model (EMEP MSC-West / Norwegian Meteorological Institute); ECMWF ERA5 meteorological driver; European Monitoring and Evaluation Programme (EMEP); Critical Loads database (CCE); CEIP emission inventories
column12: Nitrogen deposition is modelled via the EMEP atmospheric dispersion model which explicitly uses ERA5 meteorological data (wind fields, precipitation, atmospheric stability) to calculate wet and dry deposition. The ECMWF meteorological driver is a direct input. Annual rainfall variability significantly affects wet nitrogen deposition. Score 2: meteorological data are a direct model input.

column2: Fertiliser use (nitrogen) (GB)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: AHDB / Defra Fertiliser Usage Survey
column12: N fertiliser use is primarily agronomic/economic; wetter or cooler seasons can reduce application and uptake efficiency, giving moderate climate dependence.

column2: Food price volatility (UK Consumer Price Index – food)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: ONS Consumer Prices Index
column12: Food price volatility is partly driven by climate extremes in global producing regions; provides a contextual indicator of climate-related supply chain vulnerability.

column2: GHG emission intensity of electricity generation in Europe
column8: EU Electricity Market Directive; EU ETS; EU Climate Law 2021; 8th EAP mitigation objective; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: ENTSO-E electricity generation data; national GHG inventories (electricity sector); Eurostat energy statistics
column12: GHG intensity of electricity varies with weather because renewables (wind, solar, hydro) displace fossil generation in good weather years. Low-wind years and drought years increase fossil backup and raise the emissions intensity. The indicator reflects the weather-dependent fuel mix without explicitly correcting for it. Score 2: weather is a significant inter-annual confounder through the renewable generation mix.

column2: GHG emissions and removals from land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF)
column7: MtCO₂e/year net removals/emissions from LULUCF sector
column8: EU LULUCF Regulation 2018 (Regulation 2018/841); EU Climate Law 2021 (−310 MtCO₂e target 2030); 8th EAP mitigation objective; EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Annual EU GHG Inventory LULUCF sector (EEA/DG CLIMA); national forest inventories; Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS); FAO/IPCC Tier 2 methods
column12: LULUCF carbon flux modelling incorporates temperature and rainfall effects on tree growth rates, soil respiration and peatland decomposition. National carbon accounting models (e.g., CBM-CFS3, EFISCEN) use climate parameters to project growth increments. Extreme drought years visibly reduce forest carbon sinks in the annual inventory. Score 2: climate data are embedded in the underlying carbon models.

column2: Greenhouse gas removals by forests
column8: UK Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2025; Environment Act 2021 species targets; Restore and enhance nature's contributions to people
column9: Forestry Commission / Forest Research; DESNZ UK GHG Inventory LULUCF
column12: Forest carbon flux is modelled using forest inventory data and carbon accounting models. Temperature and rainfall affect tree growth rates and hence carbon accumulation; the Forestry Commission carbon models (e.g., C-FLOW, Forest Yield) incorporate climate-adjusted growth parameters.

column2: Household food insecurity prevalence (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: FSA/Food Foundation Food Insecurity Tracker; ONS HBAI
column12: Household food insecurity is amplified by climate-driven food price shocks; CCC identifies this as a key vulnerability metric. Climate is a moderate direct driver alongside socioeconomic factors.

column2: Industrial energy consumption per unit output (energy intensity)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: DESNZ Energy Consumption in the UK (ECUK)
column12: Industrial energy intensity from ECUK; process energy use is largely weather-independent but heating-related energy in some sub-sectors varies with temperature; indirect influence.

column2: Land area used for crops (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra June Survey of Agriculture
column12: Cropland area is primarily driven by economics and policy (BPS/ELMS transition). Climate indirectly influences area decisions as suitability of land shifts.

column2: Land area used for energy crops (England)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra / NNFCC
column12: Energy crop yields (Miscanthus, SRC willow) are moderately sensitive to drought and temperature; area deployed is primarily driven by BECCS and bioenergy policy demand.

column2: Land area used for livestock (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra June Survey of Agriculture
column12: Grassland area partly responsive to drought and soil moisture deficit; primarily driven by farm economics and subsidy structure.

column2: Methane emissions from agriculture
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: NAEI (DESNZ)
column12: Enteric fermentation and manure management CH₄ are directly influenced by livestock numbers and housing conditions; temperature and precipitation affect seasonal grazing patterns and anaerobic conditions in manure storage, moderately influencing annual emissions.

column2: Milk emissions intensity (UK)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: NAEI / AHDB
column12: Dairy system efficiency is influenced by feed quality and herd health, both moderately sensitive to climatic conditions.

column2: New hedgerow planting (England)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra / EA hedgerow surveys
column12: Hedgerow establishment success and survival are moderately climate-dependent via moisture availability and frost during establishment. Provides co-benefits for biodiversity and reduces runoff but planting rates primarily driven by policy/funding.

column2: Nitrous oxide emissions from agriculture
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: NAEI (DESNZ)
column12: N₂O from soils is highly sensitive to soil moisture and temperature via nitrification/denitrification; wetter and warmer conditions increase emissions. However, the dominant driver is fertiliser application rate, placing this at medium climate dependence.

column2: River and floodplain restoration — free-flowing rivers progress
column7: Number of barriers removed; km of free-flowing rivers restored; % of rivers meeting NRL restoration targets
column8: Nature Restoration Law 2024 (restore 25,000 km of free-flowing rivers by 2030); EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030; Water Framework Directive; EU Floods Directive; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: AMBER Barrier Atlas (atlas of barriers to river connectivity); national river barrier removal registries; EEA Waterbase; Joint Research Centre hydrological modelling
column12: Free-flowing river connectivity is assessed using hydrological models that incorporate river flow regimes — directly influenced by precipitation and snowmelt. Barrier removal increases natural flow variability, making rivers more climate-resilient. Hydrological models use precipitation and temperature inputs to assess ecological status. Score 2: climate data embedded in hydrological assessment models.

column2: Soil organic carbon (correlative model)
column8: Kunming-Montreal GBF: Relevant to GBF Goal A (biodiversity status and trends) and GBF monitoring framework headline indicators. Informs IPBES Global Assessment chapters on status and trends of nature for SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water).
column9: https://ipbes.net/global-assessment
column12: Soil organic carbon decomposition rates are strongly temperature-dependent; precipitation affects carbon inputs through plant productivity; correlative model uses climate as a predictor.

column2: Soil organic carbon stocks in European croplands
column7: t C/ha mean organic carbon content in 0–30cm topsoil; trend direction
column8: EU Soil Strategy 2030 (no net soil organic carbon loss by 2030; net increase target); EU Carbon Removal Certification Framework; Nature Restoration Law 2024; Farm to Fork Strategy; Restore 30% of degraded ecosystems; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity; Sustainable agriculture, aquaculture, forestry and fisheries
column9: LUCAS Soil survey (JRC/Eurostat); ESDAC European Soil Data Centre; national soil monitoring networks; Copernicus Global Land Service
column12: Soil organic carbon stocks are influenced by temperature (controlling decomposition rates) and precipitation (controlling plant inputs and moisture). SOC models (RothC, CENTURY) used to project trends explicitly use temperature and rainfall as inputs. The LUCAS Soil survey measures current stocks but future projections require climate data. Score 2: climate data embedded in SOC modelling frameworks.

column2: UK crop import ratio: cereals
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Defra UK Food Security Report / HMRC trade statistics
column12: Import ratio reflects domestic harvest variability (weather-sensitive) and trade patterns; climate moderately influences cereal yields and hence import requirements.

column2: Water leakage from public supply networks (England and Wales)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 (s.58 National Adaptation Programmes); Third National Adaptation Programme (NAP3) 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Ofwat annual leakage return
column12: Leakage levels affect climate resilience of supply during drought; pipe failures can be influenced by soil shrink-swell under dry summers. Statutory target.

column2: Woodland under sustainable management (England)
column8: UK Climate Change Act 2008 carbon budgets; Carbon Budget Delivery Plan 2023; Minimise climate change impacts on biodiversity
column9: Forestry Commission
column12: Management practices affect carbon stocks, resilience to drought and pests. Climate moderately affects the need for interventions but not the proportion managed.
